title: Demonstratives and Determiners
summary: The words that point — this, that, such, which — and those that quantify — all, every, nobody. They are adjectives in their behaviour: they decline and they agree, and the learner who has ¶17 has most of them already.

rules.heading: Šis and Tas
rules.statement: **Šis** points at what is near — *this*; **tas** at what is further off or already spoken of — *that*. Both decline and agree with their noun in gender, number and case, exactly as an adjective does (¶17). Their endings are largely the adjective endings; what has to be learnt is the short stem and the handful of forms that do not follow it.

paradigms.caption: šis and tas, singular
paradigms.footnote: In the plural: *šie, šios* and *tie, tos* in the nominative; *šių, tų* in the genitive; *šiuos, šias* and *tuos, tas* in the accusative.

examples.gloss: This flat is bigger than that one.

examples.note: genitive of negation, the demonstrative agreeing

examples.gloss: My brother lives in that house.

rules.heading: Anas: the Further Demonstrative
rules.statement: Lithuanian has a **third** degree of pointing that English lacks. **Anas** is *that one over there* — further off than *tas*, or the second of two already contrasted. It declines like *geras*, with no irregularity at all, and it is much the rarest of the three.

examples.target: Šis namas naujas, o anas senas.
examples.gloss: This house is new, and that one over there is old.

footnotes: In speech *šitas* is often heard for *šis*; it is the colloquial form of the same word and declines like *geras*.

rules.heading: Toks: Such
rules.statement: **Toks, tokia** is *such* or *of that kind*, and it is the answer to *koks?* (¶51) as *tas* is the answer to *kuris?*. Note the idiom **Koks tu geras!** — *how kind of you* — where Lithuanian uses the question word for an exclamation, and **toks** answers it.

examples.gloss: I want the same sort of book.
I do not like weather like this.

rules.heading: Kuris: Which of Several
rules.statement: **Kuris, kuri** asks *which one* out of a known set, where **koks** asks *what kind*. The distinction is real and English blurs it: *which book?* is *kuri knyga?* if the books are before you and *kokia knyga?* if you are asking what sort of book it was. **Kelintas** asks the position in an order — *the how-manieth* (¶82).

rows.label: koks
cells: Kokia tai knyga? — What sort of book is it?

rows.label: kuris
cells: Kurią knygą skaitai? — Which book are you reading?

rows.label: kelintas
cells: Kelinta valanda? — What time is it?

examples.gloss: Which bus goes to the centre?
Which floor do you live on?

rules.heading: Visas and Kiekvienas
rules.statement: **Visas** in the singular is *the whole*; in the plural, **visi, visos**, it is *all*. **Kiekvienas** is *each, every*, and being a distributive it is always **singular**, however many people are meant — in this it agrees with English *every* and not with *all*.

examples.gloss: They have all come back already.
Every week I go to the classes.

rules.heading: Niekas and the Doubled Negative
rules.statement: **Niekas** is *nobody* and *nothing* together; its genitive **nieko** is met oftener than its nominative, because a negated verb governs the genitive (¶26). The rule that governs it is the one already given for *niekada* (¶41): a negative word requires the **verb to be negated as well**. Lithuanian doubles its negatives where English forbids it, and a single negative in such a sentence is simply wrong.

paradigms.caption: The negative words and their doubling

rows.label: never
cells: I have never been to Kaunas.

paradigms.footnote: Three negatives in one clause are perfectly ordinary: *Niekas niekada nieko nesakė* — nobody ever said anything.

examples.gloss: I was at the shop but bought nothing.

rules.heading: Tas Pats: the Same
rules.statement: *The same* is **tas pats, ta pati** — literally *that itself* — and **both** words decline, each agreeing with the noun. English has one invariable word here and Lithuanian has two variable ones, so the phrase repays a moment's attention. Beside it stands **kitas**, *other* or *another* (¶98), which is its opposite.

paradigms.caption: tas pats declined
paradigms.footnote: The *č* of *paties, pačios* is the softening of *t* before a back vowel, met for the fourth time now (¶28, ¶90, ¶117).

examples.gloss: We live in the same house.

vocabulary.notes: Feminine ta; declines and agrees like an adjective.
Genitive nieko; requires the verb to be negated as well.
Requires the verb to be negated as well.

drills.stem: What is the accusative singular feminine of **šis**?
drills.explanation: *šią*. *šį* is the masculine accusative, *šios* the feminine genitive, *šioje* the feminine locative.

drills.stem: Complete: **____ autobusas važiuoja į centrą?** (Which bus goes to the centre?)
drills.explanation: **Kuris** asks which one out of a known set — the buses at the stop. *Koks* would ask what **kind** of bus it is.
A negative word requires the verb to be negated as well: *Niekas neatėjo*. Lithuanian doubles its negatives where English forbids it.

drills.stem: **Kurią knygą skaitai?** and **Kokią knygą skaitai?** — what is the difference?
options: The first asks which of the books before you; the second asks what sort of book it is.
The first is polite and the second familiar.
drills.explanation: *kuris* selects from a known set, *koks* asks after quality or kind. English says *which* for both and gives the learner no help.

drills.stem: Complete: **____ savaitę einu į kursus.** (Every week I go to the classes.)
drills.explanation: *kiekvienas* is a distributive and is always singular; the accusative of recurring occasions gives *kiekvieną savaitę*. *Visą savaitę* would mean *for the whole week*.
The second leaves the verb unnegated, which is impossible: *niekas, niekur, niekada* all require *ne-* on the verb beside them.

drills.stem: Complete: **Mes gyvename ____ name.** (We live in the same house.)
drills.explanation: *name* is a locative, and **both** words of *tas pats* must follow it into that case: *tame pačiame*. English has one invariable word here and Lithuanian two variable ones.
The negated imperative puts its object in the genitive, and the demonstrative agrees with it: *šios knygos*. Two rules act at once, and the demonstrative follows the noun wherever the noun goes.

options: *Anas* points at something further off than *tas*.
*Tas pats* declines only in its first word.
drills.explanation: Both words of *tas pats* decline — *to paties*, *tam pačiam*, *tame pačiame* — each agreeing with the noun. Lithuanian's three degrees of pointing, *šis, tas, anas*, are one more than English has.

drills.stem: **Niekas niekada nieko nesakė.** How many negative words does the sentence contain?
drills.explanation: Four: *niekas*, *niekada*, *nieko* and the *ne-* of *nesakė*. English would allow exactly one; Lithuanian requires that every negative word be accompanied by a negated verb, and piling them up is perfectly ordinary.

drills.title: Kuriame name?
drills.passage:
– Atsiprašau, kuriame name gyvena Petras?
– Tame pačiame, kuriame ir aš. Šitas namas naujas, o anas, prie parduotuvės, senas. Petras gyvena šiame, trečiame aukšte.
– Ačiū. Vakar skambinau, bet niekas neatsakė.
– Vakar jo nebuvo. Jis kiekvieną šeštadienį važiuoja pas mamą ir grįžta tik sekmadienį.
– Tokia tvarka? Tada ateisiu rytoj.
– Ateikite. Bet visą rytą jo nebus — jis dirba iki pirmos.
drills.translation: "Excuse me, which house does Petras live in?" — "The same one I do. This house is new, and that one over there, by the shop, is old. Petras lives in this one, on the third floor." — "Thank you. Yesterday I rang, but nobody answered." — "He wasn't there yesterday. Every Saturday he goes to his mother's and doesn't come back until Sunday." — "Is that the routine? Then I'll come tomorrow." — "Do. But all morning he won't be in — he works until one."

questions.explanation: *trečiame aukšte* — the ordinal in the locative, agreeing with *aukšte* as an adjective does (¶81).

questions.stem: Which words in the dialogue point at something — that is, are demonstratives?
questions.explanation: *kiekvieną* quantifies rather than points: it distributes over Saturdays. The other three are the three degrees of pointing — the same one, this one, and that one over there.

questions.stem: How many negated verbs does the dialogue contain?
questions.explanation: Three: *neatsakė*, *nebuvo* and *nebus*. The first is required by *niekas* beside it — a negative word cannot stand with an unnegated verb (¶132) — and the other two are ordinary negatives of *būti* in the past and the future.
